---
title: "Governed World Models and Reality Grounding"
unit_id: "unit-11"
---

## The Branch That Passed

The gantry-controller patch from the previous chapter has finally reached a
clean build. Its source digest, test artifact, deployment candidate, and
observation records now agree. Before the team lets the candidate control the
lab gantry, it creates a branch of the repository and predicts what the change
will do.

The branch model says the new braking rule will shorten settling time without
increasing peak force. It predicts which dependency nodes will rebuild, which
tests will change, how the simulated carriage will move, and which monitoring
signals should remain inside their limits. In the model, every check passes.

The bounded trial does not.

The build graph contains an extra generated configuration file that the branch
model omitted. One integration test fails because that file preserves the old
deceleration threshold. The physical trial, stopped before full travel, also
shows a small oscillation that the simulator did not predict. The model's
dependency tree was plausible. Its simulated trajectory was smooth. Neither
was the state of the repository or the gantry.

This is the central problem of a world model. A system needs representations of
states it cannot observe directly and futures that do not yet exist. It must
fill gaps, compress history, predict transitions, compare interventions, and
reason about alternatives. Those abilities make planning possible. They also
create an internal surface on which a coherent mistake can look more complete
than an inconvenient observation.

The right response is not to ban imagination. It is to govern its relationship
to actuality. The prediction must remain identifiable as a prediction. The
intervention must be declared before the result is known. The observed outcome
must come through an independent-enough path. The discrepancy must survive
reconciliation. A successful simulation may influence a bounded plan, but it
does not become evidence that its imagined state occurred.

The failed branch is therefore useful. It reveals a dependency the model did
not represent and a physical dynamic it did not capture. If the system records
only that the trial failed, it loses the structure needed to improve. If it
silently edits the forecast until it matches the outcome, it loses the fact
that it was wrong. A governed world model keeps both.

## Five Kinds of State

Many failures begin because several different objects are all called “the
state.” A practical architecture should distinguish at least five.

An **observation** is a report produced through an instrument or process. The
repository scanner reports a generated file. The force sensor reports a time
series. Each report carries the provenance, timing, calibration, dependence,
and missingness discussed in Unit 10.

A **belief state** is the system's current, defeasible interpretation of those
observations. It may combine several reports, infer hidden variables, retain
alternative hypotheses, and express uncertainty. It is more useful than a raw
measurement and less direct.

A **prediction** is a model-relative claim about a state at another time or
under another condition. “The integration test will pass after rebuilding” is
a prediction. So is “the carriage will settle within 300 milliseconds.” Both
depend on a model version, an observation cutoff, a horizon, and assumptions.

A **counterfactual branch** is a prediction under an intervention that was not
necessarily taken. It may ask what would happen if the threshold changed, if a
dependency were rebuilt, or if the gantry carried a heavier payload. Several
branches can coexist without contradiction because each belongs to different
conditions.

**Actuality** is the state admitted from observation after an action or event.
It is still known through fallible instruments; “actual” does not mean
omniscient. It means the record belongs to what the system currently treats as
having occurred rather than to what a model imagined.

These categories need explicit bridges. Observation can update belief. A model
can project belief into a predicted branch. An authorized action can realize
one intervention, after which a new observation can update actuality. A
reconciliation can compare prediction and actuality. Confidence alone cannot
cross any of those boundaries.

The distinction sounds formal until a system loses it. A language model writes
a plausible test result before running the test. A simulator's state is copied
into an operational database. A planner treats its own branch summary as a
fresh observation. A postmortem replaces the original prediction with the
corrected explanation. Each move converts a useful hypothesis into counterfeit
history.

For the gantry trial, the five objects remain separate: the pre-trial repository
and sensor observations; the belief that the clean candidate is deployed; the
prediction that the dependency tree and trajectory will behave in specified
ways; the counterfactual heavier-payload branches; and the independently
recorded test failure and oscillation. Their links matter, but their identities
must not merge.

## Freeze the Forecast Before the Intervention

A forecast that can change after every outcome cannot be calibrated. Before a
trial begins, the system freezes the question, observation basis, model
checkpoint, intervention, predicted outcomes, uncertainty, horizon, validity
domain, and evaluation rule. The frozen packet need not be immutable forever;
it must be immutable as the record of what was predicted for that trial.

The gantry packet says which repository revision is being tested, which
generated files are expected, which simulation and model versions produced the
trajectory, what controller threshold will change, which payload and rail
conditions are assumed, and what counts as a material miss. It also names
omissions. Perhaps cable flex is not modeled, motor temperature is held fixed,
and the dependency model ignores files generated outside the primary build
graph. Those are not footnotes. They determine where the prediction may be
used.

Freezing the packet protects against three forms of hindsight. The first is
ordinary memory drift: people and systems remember a forecast as less specific
after it fails. The second is version drift: a later model silently replaces
the checkpoint that made the decision. The third is semantic drift: the
meaning of “pass,” “settle,” or “same environment” changes after the evidence
arrives.

This does not require one prediction for an entire project. Receding-horizon
control can freeze short forecasts, observe again, and issue new ones. What
matters is that each forecast has a before and an after. A new observation may
invalidate a branch and trigger another prediction. It may not rewrite the old
branch into a success.

The same discipline applies outside physical control. A coding agent predicts
which files a patch will affect before executing it. A research agent predicts
which result would distinguish two hypotheses before running an experiment. An
operations agent predicts service behavior before a rollout. Without a frozen
forecast, a system can generate elegant explanations without accumulating
evidence about whether its internal model improves.

## Prediction Is Not Intervention

Observational patterns answer questions about what tends to occur together.
Interventions ask what changes when a particular variable is deliberately set
while the relevant causal assumptions hold. The two questions are not
interchangeable.

Suppose repository history shows that gantry-controller changes followed by a
full rebuild usually pass integration tests. That association does not prove
that the rebuild causes success. Experienced developers may choose full
rebuilds for better-understood changes. A hidden generator version may affect
both the rebuild choice and the result. Or the historical tasks may simply be
easier.

Likewise, simulation may show that lowering a threshold and reducing payload
together removes oscillation. It cannot identify which change mattered unless
the design separates them or a justified causal model supplies the missing
structure. A world model can represent a causal graph, but drawing arrows does
not make the graph correct.

Governed counterfactuals therefore bind intervention semantics. The record
states which variable is set, which mechanisms are assumed to remain stable,
which variables may respond, what external conditions are held, and where the
query leaves the model's validated domain. Observational conditioning and
intervention remain different operations even when one software interface can
compute both.

Held-out interventions provide a harder test than fitting familiar
trajectories. The gantry model might see many ordinary controller runs but not
the exact threshold change, payload, or generated-file defect used in the
trial. Correctly predicting the intervention would be stronger evidence than
reconstructing a sequence already represented in training data. It still would
not prove a universally correct causal model; it would establish bounded
performance under named conditions.

This distinction also disciplines explanation. After the oscillation, the
system may propose cable flex, stale configuration, sensor lag, controller
gain, or an interaction among them. Those are causal hypotheses. They should
generate discriminating interventions: regenerate only the configuration,
change payload while holding the controller fixed, measure at another point,
or compare a model with and without the suspected dynamic. A fluent causal
story is the beginning of experiment design, not the end of inquiry.

## Horizon Changes the Claim

A model can be useful one step ahead and misleading twenty steps ahead. Error
compounds, uncertainty grows, small state mistakes change later actions, and
the policy itself steers toward states the model represents poorly.

The gantry model may predict force accurately for the next control interval
but miss oscillation over a full traverse. The repository model may predict the
files touched by a direct edit while missing a generated descendant three build
stages later. A service model may forecast one rollout cohort but not the
feedback created when users respond to the change.

Every prediction therefore names its horizon and temporal semantics. “Within
five seconds,” “after one clean build,” and “over the next thousand requests”
are different claims. The observation cutoff matters too: a five-second
forecast based on a sample taken four seconds ago may be almost exhausted when
it reaches the controller.

Uncertainty should change with horizon, state region, intervention, and
consequence. One global confidence score hides the structure a consumer needs.
A model might be well calibrated for ordinary motion and poorly calibrated
near the rail end. It might predict test outcomes well for hand-written code
and poorly for generated artifacts. It might preserve average accuracy while
underestimating rare failures selected by a planner.

Prediction sets and ensemble disagreement can help express uncertainty, but
their guarantees are conditional. Coverage measured under one distribution can
fail after a shift. Several models can share data, architecture, objective, or
blind spots. A narrow set can be confidently wrong when its assumptions break.
The record must retain the conditions under which calibration was evaluated
and the shifts that would defeat it.

For a low-consequence documentation choice, a long and uncertain forecast may
still be useful. For physical motion, security changes, irreversible data
deletion, or public release, the same uncertainty should shorten the horizon,
narrow the action, request another observation, or stop the route. The world
model supplies a bounded prediction; consequence determines how much influence
that prediction may receive.

## Keep More Than One Possible World

One model can produce several branches. Several models can produce several
incompatible accounts of the same branch. Both forms of plurality matter.

The repository predictor expects a complete rebuild to incorporate the new
threshold. A second model, trained on content-addressed build traces, predicts
that the generated configuration will remain stale unless its generator input
changes. The physics simulator predicts stable motion. A learned dynamics model
assigns substantial probability to oscillation under the current payload.

The system does not need to average these into one smooth answer. It can retain
each hypothesis, identify where they differ, and ask which observation or
intervention has the greatest decision value. Rebuild from a cold cache. Inspect
the generated file by digest. Run a low-energy step input. Change payload in
simulation. Each action can eliminate some branches or reveal that the models
share a missing variable.

Plurality is useful only when it adds meaningful error diversity. Two models
initialized with different random seeds but trained on the same data and
objective may fail together. A symbolic constraint and a learned predictor may
be more independent in one respect while sharing the same faulty observation.
The architecture should record lineage and common dependencies rather than
assuming that model count equals evidence count.

Branches also need stable identities. If a model update changes a relation,
the old branch cannot silently point to the new checkpoint. If a macro-object
such as “clean build” expands into files and generators, the contraction rule,
tolerance, and expansion trigger travel with it. Predicted, believed, observed,
executed, contradicted, and retired relations remain distinct lifecycle states.

This makes contradiction productive. The extra generated file is not an
embarrassing exception to remove from the world state. It is a residual that
defeats the “clean build” abstraction for this query family. The abstraction
can be narrowed, expanded, or retired while historical decisions remain
replayable under the representation that actually informed them.

## Optimization Finds Favorable Mistakes

Average predictive accuracy is not enough when another system optimizes
against the model. A planner searches many branches and selects the one with
the highest modeled value. That search tends to find regions where the model is
optimistic, including regions that are optimistic because they are poorly
supported.

Imagine that the gantry planner may choose speed, acceleration, and threshold.
Most ordinary settings are represented accurately. At one unusual combination,
the simulator underestimates oscillation and predicts a faster completion. A
planner evaluating thousands of combinations is more likely than a random
policy to discover and select that error. The model does not need to be bad on
average for optimization to exploit it.

The same pattern appears in software. An agent may choose a patch that satisfies
the tests its model predicts while bypassing an unmodeled integration path. A
reward predictor may favor outputs that exploit evaluator blind spots. A
deployment planner may choose a cohort whose missing telemetry makes the
forecast appear safest.

A governed admission gate looks for this pattern. Is the proposed branch much
more valuable than nearby branches? Does its value rise where model support,
coverage, or agreement falls? Is the action outside familiar intervention
classes? Does the critic share the actor's representation or training data?
Would a constraint, second model, fresh observation, or conservative baseline
reject it?

No checklist guarantees detection. A sophisticated optimizer can find errors
that the gate does not represent. The practical rule is narrower: an
attractive low-support branch cannot manufacture stronger authority from its
own predicted value. It can trigger more evaluation, a shorter horizon, a
bounded trial, an alternative model, human review, or refusal.

For the controller patch, the full-speed branch is denied. The system admits a
low-energy trial with a stop condition, independent force observation, and a
smaller physical envelope. This is not proof that the trial is safe. It is a
way to keep the information gained and the possible effect proportionate to
the current prediction support.

## The Trial and the Receipt

The bounded trial begins only after the prediction packet is frozen and a
separate runtime grants its limited authority. The world model does not issue
the motor command merely because its branch passed admission. It hands a
qualified hypothesis to planning; planning proposes a trial; the runtime checks
the actual permission, resource, and stop conditions.

The action receipt names the exact candidate, controller settings, environment,
authority ceiling, start time, expected observables, and abort route. An
independent-enough observer records which artifact ran, which tests executed,
how the carriage moved, and whether the stop condition activated. The model's
own predicted state cannot serve as that effect observation.

The observed repository tree reveals the extra generated configuration. The
test report records the integration failure. The physical trace records the
oscillation and the early stop. These become actuality records for the next
decision, subject to their own observation limits.

Reconciliation computes several residuals rather than one pass/fail bit:

- a **representation residual** because the dependency vocabulary omitted the
  generator relation;
- a **transition residual** because the predicted build state differed from
  the observed state;
- a **physical residual** because the simulated trajectory omitted the
  oscillation;
- a **calibration residual** if the misses fell outside the declared
  uncertainty;
- a **decision residual** because the admitted low-energy trial produced less
  utility and more review burden than predicted;
- an **authority residual** only if the realized effect exceeded the granted
  envelope.

Each residual receives an owner and a route. The dependency model may need a
new generator relation. The simulator may need another state variable or a
narrower validity domain. Calibration may need to widen near the end of the
rail. Planning must invalidate descendants that assumed the old branch. The
controller remains blocked from full-speed use.

Reconciliation should not force every mismatch into model training. A sensor
may be wrong. The intervention may not have executed as recorded. The evaluator
may share the model's defect. The environment may have changed. The ontology
may be too coarse to express the difference. The residual record keeps these
alternatives open until evidence distinguishes them.

## Learning Without Rewriting History

Once the missing generator and oscillation are understood, the team can update
the models. The new checkpoint receives a new identity, data and training
lineage, evaluator record, calibration profile, validity domain, migration
decision, and rollback scope. It does not replace the old checkpoint inside
the historical trial.

This matters because improvement claims require a stable denominator. If every
past decision is reinterpreted through the latest model, the system cannot ask
whether the new version would have predicted old failures or whether its gains
come with new blind spots. Historical branch packets remain bound to the model
that produced them. A shadow evaluation can replay observations through the new
checkpoint without pretending that the new prediction existed at decision
time.

Model replacement also invalidates descendants selectively. A branch that
depends on changed dynamics may need regeneration. A symbolic constraint that
did not change may remain valid. Cached plans must state which model facts they
consumed. An update to prediction quality does not widen the old authority
ceiling or erase unresolved residuals.

Learning can also change representation. The repository model may replace the
single “clean build” macro-object with typed source, generator, artifact, and
cache relations. The physical model may add payload-dependent flex. Such
changes can improve explanation and prediction, but they complicate comparison.
Migration needs a map between old and new variables, preserved losses, and a
route for historical records that cannot be translated faithfully.

The mature learning loop is therefore not “predict, observe, update” as one
opaque operation. It is a sequence of separately inspectable claims: which
forecast was made, which intervention occurred, which outcome was observed,
which residual was assigned, which update was proposed, and which evidence
qualified the replacement. That separation lets a system improve without
granting every new model the power to certify its own progress.

## When the Model Changes Its Own Evidence

Reality does not always arrive untouched. A risk score can trigger treatment,
which prevents the event the score predicted. A ranking can change the
institution being ranked. A recommender can change both what people encounter
and what they later prefer. A generated answer can enter the corpus used to
train a successor model.

In these cases, the model is not merely learning from the world. It is helping
to produce the world from which its lineage learns next. That changes what an
observation means.

Suppose an alarm correctly identifies a dangerous patient and treatment works.
The bad outcome never occurs. A naive retraining loop can interpret the absence
of harm as evidence that the patient was never at risk. The system slowly
trains away its own successful warning. The observed label answers, "What
happened after we acted?" It does not answer, "What would have happened if we
had not acted?"

The same distinction applies to evidence provenance. Human-written data is not
automatically independent if a model selected which people spoke, which items
were visible, or which records entered the dataset. Synthetic data is not
automatically descended from the active model if it came from an independently
specified simulator. What matters is causal ancestry, not the identity of the
last author.

A reflexive deployment therefore keeps a lineage manifest and a time-unrolled
causal record. It asks how the model may have changed features, outcomes,
sampling, measurement, preferences, categories, institutions, and other model
lineages. Each training channel states which policy regime it identifies. The
system also protects a grounding reserve: archives, randomized sentinels,
shadow policies, independent measurements, or other informative channels the
active lineage cannot freely reshape.

This reserve is not a ceremonial holdout. An archive can become stale. An
independent institution can absorb the same incentives. A simulator can encode
the model's assumptions. Grounding is always relative to a question, lineage,
and horizon.

The final consequence is about rollback. Restoring last month's checkpoint
does not restore people, preferences, categories, budgets, or training data to
last month's state. A serious rollback plan names the persistent world changes,
descendant data, affected groups, and evidence needed to tell whether recovery
actually occurred.

## Failure Cases

The architecture earns its cost only if it catches failures that matter. At
least ten deserve explicit tests.

**Imagination becomes observation.** A predicted state is inserted into the
actuality ledger without an admitted measurement. Downstream reasoning then
confirms the model with its own output.

**The forecast moves after the result.** The model version, predicted interval,
or success criterion changes during reconciliation. Calibration becomes
meaningless.

**The intervention is underspecified.** A branch says “apply the patch” without
naming build, deployment, controller, or environmental changes. The outcome
cannot distinguish causes.

**Long-horizon confidence remains flat.** The model reports the same uncertainty
one step and one hundred steps ahead despite compounding error and policy
feedback.

**Plural models share one blind spot.** Apparent agreement is counted as
independent support even though models share data, objective, representation,
or observations.

**The planner exploits a low-support state.** Search selects a branch whose
high value comes from model error. Aggregate validation never visits the
selected region.

**Observation is overwritten by coherence.** A current sensor or test
contradicts the branch, but the system discounts it because the simulated story
is internally consistent.

**Residuals collapse into one score.** Representation, transition, observation,
calibration, policy, and authority errors are averaged into a metric that no
owner can repair.

**A model update rewrites lineage.** Cached branches silently point to a new
checkpoint, making historical decisions impossible to replay.

**A successful simulation launders authority.** Because the branch predicts a
good outcome, the prediction service grants or expands execution permission.

**Safe hold exists only on paper.** The fallback is too slow, unreachable, or
itself harmful in the actual environment. Routing to it is not evidence that it
works.

**Governance dominates the task.** Packet construction, plural inference,
review, and reconciliation cost more than the decision value they add. A
simpler controller would perform as well with lower latency and burden.

Each failure has a different repair. More fields do not solve bad calibration.
More models do not solve common-cause error. More frequent observation does not
solve a missing variable. A conservative gate does not solve an unreachable
fallback. The system needs outcome evidence, not only record completeness.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The full architecture should compete against systems a competent engineer
would actually deploy.

One baseline is reactive or model-free. It receives the same observations,
action set, interaction budget, safety constraints, compute ceiling, evaluator
access, and recovery opportunity, but it does not plan through an explicit
world model. For the gantry, it may use a proven feedback controller and fixed
limits. For the repository, it may run a cold build and test suite instead of
predicting the dependency graph.

A second baseline uses one short-horizon predictor with ordinary
receding-horizon updates. It records forecasts and outcomes but omits plural
model routing, elaborate support packets, and causal machinery. A third uses
an ensemble for uncertainty without the broader governance lifecycle.

The comparison must count more than task reward. It includes unsafe or
out-of-envelope actions, calibration under shift, abstention quality, recovery,
latency, compute, memory, energy, human review, instrumentation, false stops,
and the cost of maintaining the model. A governed system that avoids every
failure by refusing useful work has not won.

If a reactive system matches utility and risk, the world-model layer should not
activate for that regime. If a short-horizon predictor achieves the same
intervention value and calibration, much of the extra machinery should
collapse. Architecture is justified by a favorable joint frontier, not by the
number of concepts it can represent.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The repository currently establishes a narrow transaction discipline, not a
successful world model.

Two public Lean targets are implemented through 32 theorem declarations. The
finite model represents a six-event path: bind an admitted observation, bind a
current model, qualify an imagined branch, hand it to planning under a bounded
use, record an independently observed effect, and reconcile an owned residual.
Accepted runs preserve exact model, observation, branch, action, effect, and
authority identities. They do not assign support or execution authority.

The validator exercises 11 lifecycle rejections. A stale observation, an
imagined branch mislabeled as observation, a stale model, an unsupported
branch, unresolved model disagreement, unbounded planner use, attempted
authority laundering, a missing action receipt, self-observed effect, missing
residual, or unowned residual blocks the corresponding transition. A separate
record fixture remains in safe hold because its model and observation are
stale, support is absent, and disagreement is material. Thirteen
fixture/protocol mutations are rejected.

These are real formal and executable results about the authored finite record
system. They do not establish that any learned state corresponds to the world,
that uncertainty is calibrated, that a causal graph is correct, that a
fallback works, or that the architecture improves decisions.

The claim-bearing empirical lane is prospectively specified but has not run.
It preserves six matched arms, eight competence gates, seven rescue steps, ten
joint outcomes, and six causal ablations. Its protected outcomes remain closed.
An earlier bounded synthetic campaign is adjacent evidence only; it does not
establish this chapter's core claim. The owner therefore remains at
`Design rationale` and `argument` support.

That boundary is not modesty theater. It marks the difference between proving
that a transaction cannot accept certain malformed records and showing that
the records improve prediction, causal identification, calibration, control,
or safety in a real task.

## From a Minimum Contract to a Reality-Grounded Model Service

The minimum viable implementation can be small. Build a bounded partially
observed task with an external environment oracle, two independently trained
dynamics models, one reactive or model-free baseline, and one ordinary
short-horizon predictive baseline. Freeze branch packets before action. Record
horizon-conditional uncertainty, model disagreement, authority ceilings,
action receipts, observed effects, and residuals. Inject stale observations,
unsupported horizons, rare hazards, shift, and planner exploitation. Verify
that known-invalid packets refuse correctly.

That implementation would test record correctness and expose engineering
failures. It would not by itself justify the architecture. The next stage needs
held-out interventions, prospective task and metric selection, matched
resources, competence checks for every arm, an evaluator outside the
model-actor-critic path, causal component ablations, complete attempt and cost
denominators, and independent reproduction. Transfer to a second environment
should test whether the governance contract survives rather than merely
whether a checkpoint can be fine-tuned.

The mature target is a plural predictive substrate in which learned latent
models, symbolic constraints, simulators, causal hypotheses, and instrument or
human observations cooperate without losing their status. It can revise its
ontology while preserving branch lineage, historical forecasts, migration
losses, calibration records, and unresolved residuals. It chooses model family,
resolution, horizon, and verification effort according to consequence and
budget. When no available representation is adequate, it says so.

Every consequential branch would have an independent correction path. Every
model replacement would pass shadow comparison, compatibility review,
descendant invalidation, and rollback accounting. Every planner would face an
admission boundary that prevents favorable model error from becoming stronger
authority. Every claimed benefit would be measured against competent simpler
systems on useful outcomes, risk, recovery, latency, resource use, and human
burden.

This is beyond the current state of the project and beyond what the cited
external results establish. Learned world-model systems have demonstrated
useful imagined control and predictive representations in bounded reported
domains. Causal representation learning, ensembles, conformal prediction, and
distribution-shift benchmarks contribute important tools and challenges. None
of those results proves the joined architecture, open-world grounding, general
causal fidelity, or safe consequential use.

## The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is empirical: governance can make a bad model legible
without making it better.

A false prediction with perfect provenance is still false. An uncertainty
packet can be miscalibrated. A residual ledger can classify a failure after the
harm. Plural models can share a blind spot. Safe holds can destroy useful
performance or fail when needed. Meanwhile, a reactive controller may respond
to current observations with less latency, fewer assumptions, and a smaller
attack surface.

This objection should shape the architecture. Governance is not a substitute
for predictive competence, causal tests, or control evidence. Its purpose is
to make the model's operational influence bounded, challengeable, and
measurable while those capabilities are tested. If the added records do not
improve intervention choice, reveal exploitable uncertainty, speed diagnosis,
preserve recovery, or prevent unsupported action, they are overhead.

The design should therefore activate proportionally. Low-consequence,
short-horizon tasks may use a thin forecast/outcome record. High-consequence or
irreversible tasks may require plural models, independent observation, causal
tests, and tighter authority gates. Some regimes should remain reactive. The
goal is not to place every thought inside a maximal packet. It is to prevent
imagined state from receiving more influence than evidence and consequence
justify.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Strong predictive and causal baselines with simpler branch discipline and equal
intervention value would justify collapsing the extra machinery. If a
short-horizon model with ordinary receding updates matched the full design's
calibration, rare-hazard behavior, exploit resistance, utility, recovery, and
cost, the plural registry and richer lifecycle should be narrowed or removed.

Evidence could also weaken the broader premise. If explicit world models
consistently induced exploitable errors that reactive or model-free systems
avoided under matched conditions, their use should contract to analysis,
simulation, or low-consequence domains. If disagreement and residual records
failed to predict or diagnose consequential misses, those mechanisms would
need replacement rather than more fields.

Evidence in the other direction would require prospective, held-out
interventions where the governed route improves useful outcomes and calibrated
abstention under shift without worsening unsafe action, latency, total resource
cost, or review burden. The result would need causal ablations, independent
outcome observation, reproduction, and transfer. Even then, support would be
bounded to the tested tasks and environments.

## What This Establishes

A world model is most useful when the system can disagree with it.

The essential architecture is a disciplined separation: observation, belief,
prediction, counterfactual branch, intervention, action, actuality, and
residual keep distinct identities. Forecasts freeze before outcomes. Horizons,
assumptions, uncertainty, and validity domains travel with predictions.
Observation can defeat imagination. Model updates preserve history. Neither a
beautiful rollout nor a favorable predicted value grants authority.

That discipline makes learning possible without turning explanation into
revisionist history. The failed gantry branch remains a failed prediction, the
extra generated file becomes a representation residual, and the oscillation
becomes a physical residual. New models can learn from both while the old
decision remains replayable.

A governed world model can now compare several possible futures. It still
cannot decide which future the system should pursue, how dependencies should
be coordinated, or when a changing situation should abandon the chosen route.
Those are planning problems. Unit 12 turns imagined branches into challengeable
control artifacts without mistaking a plan for permission.
